top_choice_rationale: The magic-wavelength optical lattice clock is a genuinely new regime: many neutral atoms interrogated at once with the trapping light cancelled from the clock transition, so statistics and accuracy improve together. It has been reproduced at about 10^-18 in several independent laboratories and already yields laboratory tests of gravitational redshift, constants and dark-matter couplings, so it is mature and not a single-measurement claim. Katori (the magic-wavelength proposal and its first realisation) and Ye (the development to the 10^-18 level) are a well-scoped two-person allocation, and the citation is narrow enough to avoid overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes. No award is clearly worse than a well-founded, mature prize.
recusal_note: No direct collaboration with Katori or Ye is apparent from the profile, but she is a theoretical atomic physicist in a neighbouring precision-atomic field, with close ties to Lund and ETH attosecond groups; a possible but weak conflict, not requiring recusal as far as the profile shows.
